label: Stud Frame (Light Sawn Timber)
volunteer_identification_guide: Light dimensional studs (typically 100x50mm) spaced at 400-600mm centres with noggins, top and bottom plates, nailed together; rapid adoption after 1853 gold rush.

label: Heavy Box Frame (Mortised Posts/Beams)
volunteer_identification_guide: Traditional heavy timber framing with substantial corner posts (150-200mm square), intermediate wall posts, wall plates, and mortise-and-tenon or lap jointing.

label: Round Bush-Pole Frame
volunteer_identification_guide: Framing composed of debarked tree poles joined with notches, rebating, wire ties, and heavy spikes; standard vernacular framing for woolsheds, stables, and machinery sheds.

label: Vertical Split Timber Slab
volunteer_identification_guide: Thick split hardwood slabs set vertically into grooved or rebated top and bottom plates, often secured by timber wedges; gaps chinked with battens, hessian, or clay.

label: Horizontal Drop-Log / Slab (Slotted)
volunteer_identification_guide: Split timber slabs or round logs laid horizontally, with ends slotted into vertical grooves cut into massive upright corner and door posts; allows expansion.

label: Pise (Rammed Earth)
volunteer_identification_guide: Subsoil tamped firmly between wooden shuttering boards in sequential lifts (500-800mm high); produces thick solid earth walls (300-450mm) with visible lift lines and putlog holes.

label: Wattle & Daub / Pug & Pine
volunteer_identification_guide: Interwoven wattles/saplings or vertical cypress pine saplings plastered thickly with mud, clay, straw, and cow manure; coated with limewash.

label: Mudbrick / Sun-Dried Adobe
volunteer_identification_guide: Sun-dried bricks made of clay, silt, sand, and straw binder laid in mud mortar; walls typically rendered with lime or mud plaster.

label: Solid Brick Masonry
volunteer_identification_guide: Continuous brickwork across full wall thickness (9, 14, or 18 inches); bonded using English, Flemish, or Colonial bonds; header bricks tie exterior and interior leaves together.

label: Cavity Brick Masonry
volunteer_identification_guide: Two parallel brick leaves separated by 50mm air gap tied with iron wire or terra cotta ties; introduced widely from early 1880s to halt moisture transmission.

label: Stone Masonry Wall
volunteer_identification_guide: Solid masonry walling of ashlar blocks, squared coursed stone, or random rubble fieldstone bonded with lime mortar or clay.

label: Corrugated Iron (CGI) on Timber Frame
volunteer_identification_guide: Corrugated iron sheets nailed or screwed directly to horizontal timber wall battens or light studs; ubiquitous in pastoral sheds, shearers quarters, and outbuildings.

label: Mortise & Tenon Joint
volunteer_identification_guide: Rectangular projecting tongue (tenon) fitted snugly into rectangular socket (mortise); hallmark of traditional heavy carpentry and high-grade pre-1860 construction.

label: Pegged Timber Joint (Drawbore)
volunteer_identification_guide: Timber joint locked with round hardwood dowels/trunnels driven through offset holes, drawing joint tight without metal fixings.

label: Halving / Notched Lap Joint
volunteer_identification_guide: Half the timber thickness removed from both members to create a flush overlapping intersection; common in wall plates and top chords.

label: Bird s Mouth Rafter Notch
volunteer_identification_guide: V-shaped triangular notch cut into underside of rafter to seat securely over wall top plate, preventing roof slippage.

label: Simple Butt Joint (Face Nailed)
volunteer_identification_guide: Square-cut timber end pressed squarely against face and secured by direct nails; became standard with rise of light stud framing.

label: Hand-wrought Nails (Square Tapered)
volunteer_identification_guide: Forged by hand; features square shank tapering on all 4 sides with irregular hand-hammered rosehead or clasp head; diagnostic of pre-1860s construction.

label: Machine-cut / Ewbank Patent Nails
volunteer_identification_guide: Stamped from iron plate; shank tapers on two opposing parallel sides while remaining uniform on other two; rectangular head; dominant c. 1840-1880s.

label: Wire Nails (Round Shank, Machine Head)
volunteer_identification_guide: Manufactured from drawn steel wire; perfectly circular shank, flat round head with cross-hatched grip marks; introduced 1870s, dominant by 1890s.

label: Baling Wire / Improvised Bush Repairs
volunteer_identification_guide: Fencing wire, baling wire, or bent strap iron twisted around posts and rails; diagnostic of improvised pastoral maintenance.
